analysis.one_liner: Lets workers get a full fresh court review when their employer plan denies benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to a House committee and died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, when an employer health or retirement plan denies a benefit claim, courts often defer to the plan's decision if the plan document gives its administrators discretion. This bill would require courts to review every benefit denial from scratch — de novo — so a worker's case gets a full independent look rather than a rubber stamp of the plan's own ruling.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees in employer health and retirement plans who are denied benefits. When a plan denies a claim, they could ask a court to re-decide the question on the merits, instead of prevailing only if they could prove the plan's ruling was unreasonable.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers denied health or pension benefits

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends ERISA so that 'any benefit determination under the plan shall be subject to de novo review by the court,' regardless of any plan provision giving fiduciaries discretionary authority over benefit decisions.

It applies to cases arising after enactment, so every future benefit denial — health claims, pension payouts, disability benefits — would get a full court reconsideration rather than deferential review.

De novo review means the court decides the claim on its own judgment of the facts and terms, which removes the incentive for plans to deny borderline claims knowing their decision carries extra weight in court.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor benefit plans and the insurers and administrators that run them would face more litigation and more paid claims, since courts could second-guess denials. Plans would likely pay more in benefits and legal costs, which could in some cases be passed to employers or workers as premium or plan costs.

drawbacks.text: Plans would face more litigation over benefits, and employers sponsoring health or retirement plans could see higher claims and legal costs — costs that plans may pass along to employers or to workers in premiums and fees.
The bill was a one-line amendment with no hearings or committee findings on cost, so Congress never weighed the litigation burden against the fairness benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers whose claims are denied, the change is significant: it replaces deference to the plan's own decision-maker with an independent court decision, which is the difference between a real appeal and a long shot. The main honest objection is cost — more denials challenged in court means higher litigation and benefits costs for plans, and it is fair to ask who absorbs those. The bill did nothing to resolve that question; it died unexamined in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 1998 and sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and the bill expired when that Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Filner introduced the bill on August 5, 1998, near the end of the 105th Congress.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
No cosponsors signed on, and the action history shows no hearings, markups, floor action, or further committee activity before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, insurers, and plan administrators who run employee benefit plans keep the current court deference to their benefit denials, with no new litigation risk.

for.name: Rep. Bob Filner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; it was his measure alone, with no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill drew one Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and no recorded party opposition before dying in committee.

industries.industry: Employer benefit plan administrators and insurers (ERISA plans)
industries.note: De novo review strips away the court deference plans gain when they write discretionary authority into plan documents, so benefit denials can be re-decided on the merits. Keeping that deference makes it cheaper to deny borderline claims; the bill would have raised litigation and paid-claim costs.

industries.industry: Employers sponsoring health and retirement plans
industries.note: Plan sponsors could face more litigation and higher benefit payouts, costs they may ultimately share. Many sponsor plans that genuinely intend to pay benefits, so the bill's effect on them is not one-sided.
